content.text: To verify the performance increases:  (make sure you're running on a quadcore).
1.  run fcrepo-webapp with the jdbc-postgres repository.json modeshape config.
2.  git clone
https://github.com/dbernstein/fcrepo-performance-test-scripts.git
3.  execute ./n-members.sh 10000;
4.  Note the elapsed times.
5.  execute ./n-memberof.sh 10000;
6.  Note the elapsed times.
7. Clear the fcrepo-data directory and your postgresql fcrepo database.
8. copy fcrepo4/fcrepo-config/src/main/resources/config/jdbc-postgresql/respository.json to /any/path/repository.json.
9. open the file and changed the cacheSize value to 500000.
10.   run fcrepo-webapp with the -Dfcrepo.modeshape.configuration=/any/path/repository.json and add -Dfcrepo.enable-parallel-streaming-by-default=true.
11.  Rerun 3 - 6.
You should see 5-10x speed increases.
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/pull/1177
(make sure you're running on a quadcore)
Why? Why is this important?
Because the the optimization in part involves turning on parallel stream processing.   Quadcore is not necessary, but I wouldn't expect to see the most dramatic results on a single core.
So this doesn't actually address the problem of retrieving/using JCR nodes instead of identifiers?
No it does not. I did not achieve success going down that road.  It appeared to me that jcr nodes were getting loaded under the hood anyway I tried it.
Okay, then I would leave this issue open or reopen it after merge, just in case someone else wants to tackle the underlying problem.
, this looks very promising!

I've done some testing of this and do see dramatic improvement of the 10k members test script.  I tried the cacheSize config change and was still seeing ~30 seconds to edit one our largest objects (which has 1296 members, and both membership proxies and a separate resource encoding table-of-contents hierarchy of the members using hash URI resources in a single Fedora resource).  I think the difference here might be that Hydra does some inefficient things (like destroying and rebuilding that table-of-contents resource with every update to the main object).  I'm ingesting a large test object on our staging server now so I can more thoroughly test the parallel retrieval change too.
Pending response to code review comments.
Additionally, I am getting test failures when running:
mvn -Dfcrepo.enable-parallel-streaming-by-default=true clean install
..specifically:
Failed tests:
ReferencesRdfContextTest.testStrongReferences:120 null
ReferencesRdfContextTest.testWeakReferences:129 null
The tests pass with the latest update, but I did not do a full regression to test that the changes did not affect performance.
: If you're satisified with the change,  hold off on merging until I confirm that the performance gains are still valid with the unit test fix.
:  FYI performance gains still hold with the last commit.

Regarding performance, that is good... albeit surprising, to hear. Does it make sense to you that we would still be seeing the performance gains despite turning off parallelism in exactly the code that was believed to be the source of the issue?

: That's an excellent point.  I didn't realize that I turned it off right where  I had turned it on.   So yes it is surprising.  I did a quick check to make sure that the performance was still good, but I did not check it with the exact conditions of my previous tests.  So it is possible that I wasn't getting the same performance I was getting before with caching and parallel=true against postgres.  I will check again and if necessary keep working it.
:  I reverted the previous two commits and fixed the problem correctly this time.   See the latest changes to
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/pull/1177
: Looks good. Here is some minor clean-up:
https://github.com/dbernstein/fcrepo4/pull/2
Resolved with
https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/commit/cd5b69e2b8e85f13651fe7e88e88c6d7154105c6
The issue of retrieving nodes vs. retrieving IDs has not been resolved, has it?

, no — the resolution here was to make better use of Modeshape's node cache and parallelize RDF generation, so at least we're not retrieving each node and producing triples in sequence.  Refactoring triple generation to completely avoid loading the nodes is a much larger task, and one that
and
both put a lot of effort towards, but neither of those efforts was completed.  Do you want to create a follow-on ticket to revisit that?

I am of two minds about that myself.  Part of me thinks it would be very good for the long-term health of Fedora-on-Modeshape to do that.  But the other part thinks that putting effort into alternate implementations might be a better use of our limited resources.
I would open a new ticket to describe what

did here and keep this one open. Danny's work is excellent, but it doesn't solve the problem at the root of this ticket. I'm perfectly well aware that some of the best people who have worked on this software failed to solve that problem. That's why I would want to leave this ticket open-- as a warning.
I have been testing the performance of Fedora objects that link to many other repository objects (for example a collection with many members, or a book that contains many pages).

I've written up some of my findings in the Fedora wiki[1].  But the TL;DR version is that it's reasonably fast for small numbers of members, but gets progressively slower for larger numbers of members.  And the move from LevelDB to a relational database for storing metadata looks like it's adding to this issue.  So a book with 500+ pages or a collection that contains thousands of objects slows down to 30+ seconds to read the RDF from Fedora.
I mostly wanted to let people know about this issue so it can be a factor in discussions about modeling, performance, etc.
-Esmé
https://wiki.duraspace.org/display/FF/Real+World+Performance#RealWorldPerformance-many_members
